title: What's gone wrong at Britain's worst bathing site?
summary: The BBC looks at why in a dry summer with few sewage spills, one bathing site failed so many water quality tests.

Figure caption, 'Within six hours I was unwell': Was wastewater to blame? By Jonah Fisher , Environment correspondent and Tom Ingham, Josh Falcon, Tony Jolliffe , Climate and Science team Published 18 November 2026 The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim. But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together. "People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge. People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years. But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA). Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor. "There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything." "This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps. "I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day." So why is she back swimming in it? "There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says. Britain's Worst Bathing Site Inside the bathing site designated the worst in the UK Watch on iPlayer Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBC Image caption, The BBC has been investigating whether discharges of treated sewage might be responsible for poor water quality at a bathing site in Taunton. This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites. The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria – E. coli and intestinal enterococci – that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested. So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works. We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies. Image source, Jonah Fisher/BBC Image caption, Despite the high levels of faecal bacteria and the health warnings, Jenny, Jo and Jo have kept swimming at the bathing site in Taunton The testing regime Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish. The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested – so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness. As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers. We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer. That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river. Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes. Why are our rivers so dirty? Last year the official advice was not to swim at 12 of the 14 inland river bathing sites in England . Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers? In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river. So the BBC carried out its own sampling near three wastewater treatment works upstream of the Taunton site. We found the treated liquid coming out of the nearest sewage works at Bradford-on-Tone had about 240,000 colony forming units (CFU) of E. coli per 100ml - that's a level about 250 times higher than that considered safe for swimming. "The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate. What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone. It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit. "You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says. "If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river." We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Enginee
